title: Repairs in Rental Properties
text:
Urgent repairs are repairs that make a rental property unsafe or difficult to live in and are legally defined under Victorian rental law.
Non-urgent repairs are repairs that are not classified as urgent. A repair is generally non-urgent when the renter can continue to safely live in the property.
Examples of non-urgent repairs can include a broken dishwasher or loose bathroom tiles.
Rental providers must arrange urgent repairs immediately. Non-urgent repairs must generally be completed within 14 days after receiving a written repair request.

title: Repairs in Rental Properties
text:
The Consumer Affairs Victoria urgent-repair list includes issues such as:
- Burst water services
- Blocked or broken toilet systems
- Serious roof leaks
- Gas leaks
- Dangerous electrical faults
- Flooding or serious flood damage
- Serious storm or fire damage
- Failure of essential hot water, water, cooking, heating or laundering services/appliances
- Failure of gas, electricity or water supply
- Failure of a cooling appliance or service provided by the rental provider
- The property not meeting minimum rental standards
- A non-working safety device such as a smoke alarm or pool fence
- Certain appliances, fittings or fixtures causing significant water wastage
- Faults or damage making the property unsafe or insecure, including certain structural pests, mould or damp issues
- Serious problems with a lift or staircase

title: Repairs in Rental Properties
text:
Renters should notify the rental provider or property manager in writing about repairs as soon as possible.
For urgent repairs, the renter should contact the rental provider or agent immediately, including using the emergency contact number provided when they moved in. The renter should also confirm the request in writing and keep evidence of the request.
For non-urgent repairs, the request should be in writing and include the date of the request.

title: Repairs in Rental Properties
text:
The rental provider generally organises and pays for repairs when the damage or fault was not caused by the renter.
If the renter caused the damage, the renter may be responsible for the repair costs.
Where repairs require a licence or registration, the work must be completed by a suitably qualified person. Repairs must be completed to the standard expected of a tradesperson.

title: Repairs in Rental Properties
section_title: URGENT REPAIRS PAID FOR BY THE RENTER
text:
If a rental provider or agent does not respond promptly to an urgent repair request, a renter may arrange and pay for the repair themselves when the repair costs $2,500 or less.
The renter should keep receipts and provide written notice requesting reimbursement. The rental provider must reimburse the renter within 7 days of receiving the written notice.
For urgent repairs costing more than $2,500, the renter should not arrange and pay for the repair themselves. They should seek assistance through Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria (RDRV).

title: Repairs in Rental Properties
text:
If a rental provider does not complete a non-urgent repair within 14 days of the written request, the renter has options to seek further assistance.
A renter can request a repairs inspection from Consumer Affairs Victoria. The renter may also apply to VCAT if the required repairs have not been completed within the relevant timeframe.

title: Repairs in Rental Properties
text:
Renters must continue paying rent while waiting for repairs to be completed or while waiting for reimbursement for repairs.
In some circumstances, a renter can apply for rent to be paid into a Rent Special Account while a repair-related issue is being resolved.

title: Repairs in Rental Properties
section_title: WHEN THE RENTER CAUSED THE DAMAGE
text:
If the renter caused a fault or damage, the rental provider can require the renter to repair the damage or pay for the repair.
The rental provider must provide a written repair notice explaining the damage, that the renter caused it, and whether the renter is expected to arrange the repair or whether the rental provider will arrange it.
If the renter is required to organise the repair, it generally must be completed within 14 days and to a tradesperson standard.

title: Repairs in Rental Properties
text:
Renters and rental providers should first try to resolve repair issues by communicating with each other.
Consumer Affairs Victoria provides a free repairs inspection service in relevant circumstances.
Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria (RDRV) is a free alternative dispute resolution service that can assist with rental disputes.
If a dispute cannot be resolved through RDRV, the matter may proceed to VCAT where appropriate.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
section_title: BOND CLAIMS AT THE END OF A RENTAL AGREEMENT
text:
When a rental agreement ends, renters and rental providers make a bond claim to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA).
A bond claim tells the RTBA how the bond should be repaid.
Bond money is generally returned to renters when they move out unless there is a valid reason for the rental provider to claim some or all of the bond.
Bonds cannot be claimed to pay rent during an ongoing rental agreement.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
section_title: REASONS A RENTAL PROVIDER MAY CLAIM BOND
text:
A rental provider may claim compensation from the bond because the renter:
- Damaged the property
- Owes rent or other charges after the rental agreement has ended
- Did not leave the property reasonably clean
- Is responsible for missing items, such as locks
- Made certain changes to the property without permission
A rental provider cannot claim bond for fair wear and tear or for damage that was the rental provider's responsibility to repair.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
A final inspection is carried out at the end of the rental agreement.
The condition report should be used to compare the condition of the property at the beginning and end of the rental agreement.
The renter must either:
- Be present during the final inspection, or
- Have been given a reasonable opportunity to attend
Photographs taken at the beginning of the rental agreement can also provide evidence of the property's original condition.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
Rental providers cannot claim bond to cover fair wear and tear.
Fair wear and tear is deterioration resulting from:
- Reasonable use of the property
- Natural environmental forces
Examples may include faded curtains or worn kitchen benchtops.
Damage such as ripped curtains or broken benchtops may be treated differently from fair wear and tear.
If renters and rental providers disagree about whether something is reasonable wear and tear or damage, they can seek dispute resolution.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
If a renter owes rent after the rental agreement has ended, the rental provider may claim the amount owed from the bond.
The bond cannot be used to pay rent while the rental agreement is still ongoing.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
Sometimes renters and rental providers disagree about how the bond should be distributed.
For example, a renter may believe:
- They did not cause the alleged damage
- The damage existed before the rental agreement
- The issue is fair wear and tear
- The amount claimed by the rental provider is not appropriate
Renters and rental providers are encouraged to negotiate and try to reach an agreement.
If the parties cannot agree, a party may seek assistance through Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria (RDRV) or apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT), depending on the applicable process.
An applicable legally binding order can be submitted to the RTBA, which will distribute the bond according to the order.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
section_title: CLAIMING A BOND THROUGH THE RTBA
text:
Bond claims are made using the RTBA online system.
A rental provider must start a claim with the RTBA within 14 days of the rental agreement ending unless a renter starts the claim first.
Rental providers must be registered with the RTBA to initiate a claim.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
A rental provider will usually start a bond claim after the parties have agreed on how the bond should be repaid.
When the rental provider submits the claim, each renter listed on the bond receives an email notification containing a link to review the claim.
Renters can:
- Review the proposed repayment
- Accept the claim
- Request a change if they believe something is incorrect
Renters must accept the claim within 14 days or the transaction will no longer be available to complete.
If everyone accepts the claim, the RTBA will usually repay the bond within one business day.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
Any renter whose name is listed on the bond can start a bond claim after the rental agreement ends.
The renter must authenticate their identity with Service Victoria before starting the claim.
The renter does not need to wait for the rental provider to initiate the bond claim.
When a renter starts a claim, the RTBA notifies the other parties listed on the bond.
Other parties generally have 14 days to contest the claim by making an application to VCAT or RDRV.
If nobody contests the claim, the bond is repaid according to the claim after the response period.
The bond can be repaid sooner if all parties agree.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
If another party disagrees with a renter-initiated bond claim, they can contest it through the applicable dispute process.
The party must act within the relevant response period.
If the claim is not contested within the required period, the RTBA can repay the bond according to the renter-initiated claim.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
Where a bond dispute requires a decision, an applicable legally binding order can determine how the bond should be distributed.
An order may be necessary when:
- There is a dispute about the distribution of the bond
- At least one party cannot be contacted
The relevant order or reference can be submitted as part of the RTBA bond-claim process.
Once an applicable order is validated, the RTBA can distribute the bond according to that order.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
In some circumstances, supporting documentation may need to be attached to a bond claim.
This may occur when:
- An order cannot be automatically validated
- A court other than VCAT has made an order
- Other circumstances require the RTBA to review supporting documentation
The RTBA reviews the submitted documentation before completing the bond transaction.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
During the claim process, people receiving a repayment provide their bank account details.
The RTBA pays the bond into the nominated bank account.
Australian and international bank accounts can be used.
People making a claim should carefully check their banking details because the RTBA does not retain renter banking details for verification.
If valid payment details have not been provided, the RTBA may retain the repayment until a valid payment option is provided.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
A bond may be transferred to a new rental property through the Portable Rental Bond Scheme.
The same general bond-dispute process applies to a bond that has been transferred.
The rental provider for the previous property can still make a bond claim after the bond has been transferred.
If money is payable to the previous rental provider and there is not enough bond balance remaining after the transfer, the government may pay the rental provider on the renter's behalf.
That amount then becomes a repayment owed by the renter to the State of Victoria.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
section_title: BOND CLOSURE AFTER A PORTABLE BOND TRANSFER
text:
The RTBA can close a bond when:
- Its balance is $0 after transfer to a new rental property
- The bond is not under dispute
- No claims have been submitted
People listed on the bond are notified before closure.
They generally have 14 days to dispute the closure by making an application to VCAT or RDRV and providing the relevant reference to the RTBA.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
Bonds funded by Homes Victoria are generally returned in full to Homes Victoria at the end of the rental agreement.
If a rental provider wants to claim some or all of a Homes Victoria-funded bond, they must obtain an applicable VCAT order.

title: Bond Claims and Refunds
text:
Consumer Affairs Victoria identifies the following provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 in relation to bond claims and refunds:
- Section 411AB – Matters that may be subject of bond claim
- Section 411AD – Disputed bond claims

title: Rent Increases
section_title: HOW OFTEN RENT CAN BE INCREASED
text:
For residential rental agreements that started on or after 19 June 2019, rent generally cannot be increased more than once every 12 months.
For agreements that started before 19 June 2019, different rules may apply.
A rental provider cannot increase rent during a fixed-term agreement unless the rental agreement allows for the increase.
The rental agreement should state how a permitted rent increase will be calculated.

title: Rent Increases
text:
A rental provider must generally give the renter at least 90 days' notice before a rent increase takes effect.
The notice must be given in writing using the prescribed Notice of rent increase to renter/s of rented premises form.
The notice should clearly state:
- The amount of the new rent
- How the rent increase was calculated
- What the renter can do if they believe the increase is too high
If the correct form is not used or the required notice is not provided, the rent increase notice may not be valid.

title: Rent Increases
section_title: RENT INCREASES DURING A FIXED-TERM AGREEMENT
text:
A rental provider generally cannot increase rent during a fixed-term rental agreement unless the agreement contains a term allowing the increase.
Where an increase is permitted during a fixed term, the rental agreement must explain how the increase will be calculated.
The calculation may be based on an agreed method such as:
- Consumer Price Index (CPI)
- A rent index
- A percentage
- A fixed dollar amount
The rental provider must still comply with applicable notice requirements.

title: Rent Increases
text:
The rental provider must tell the renter the amount of the proposed increase.
The notice must also explain how the increase was calculated.
This allows the renter to understand the basis for the proposed change and, where applicable, challenge the increase.

title: Rent Increases
text:
A renter who believes a proposed rent increase is too high can request a rent assessment from Consumer Affairs Victoria.
The renter must generally request the assessment within 30 days of receiving the rent increase notice.
Consumer Affairs Victoria can investigate the proposed increase and prepare a rent assessment report.
The renter and rental provider receive the assessment report.
If the renter is not satisfied and the dispute remains unresolved, the report can be used as part of the applicable rental dispute-resolution process.

title: Rent Increases
text:
A Consumer Affairs Victoria rent assessment considers whether the proposed rent is excessive.
The assessment can consider relevant information about the rental property and rental market.
If the dispute remains unresolved after the renter receives the rent assessment report, the renter can use the applicable Rental Dispute Resolution Victoria (RDRV) process.
The renter generally needs to act within the applicable timeframe after receiving the rent assessment report.
RDRV is part of Victoria's current rental dispute-resolution framework.
If a dispute cannot be resolved through the applicable RDRV process, the matter may proceed to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT), where appropriate.
Renters should follow the current instructions provided with their rent assessment report because the appropriate dispute pathway can depend on the circumstances.

title: Rent Increases
section_title: IF THE RENT INCREASE NOTICE IS INVALID
text:
A renter should check whether the rental provider:
- Used the correct prescribed form
- Provided the required 90 days' notice
- Clearly stated the increased rent
- Explained how the increase was calculated
- Included information about the renter's rights to challenge the increase
If the required information or notice is missing, the proposed increase may not be valid.

title: Rent Increases
text:
The rental agreement should contain information about rent and how permitted rent increases will be calculated.
Renters should keep copies of:
- Their rental agreement
- Rent increase notices
- Relevant emails or other communications
- Consumer Affairs Victoria rent assessment reports
- Documents relating to any dispute-resolution process
Keeping these records can help if a dispute occurs.

title: Rent Increases
text:
If a renter believes a rent increase is excessive, they can request a rent assessment from Consumer Affairs Victoria.
If the dispute is not resolved after the assessment, the renter can follow the applicable RDRV dispute-resolution process.
If the dispute remains unresolved, it may proceed to VCAT where appropriate.
Renters should continue meeting their rental agreement obligations while the dispute is being resolved unless a lawful alternative arrangement or order applies.

title: Rent Increases
text:
The minimum notice period for residential rental rent increases changed from 60 days to 90 days on 25 November 2025.
The 90-day requirement is therefore treated as the current general rule for this knowledge base as of September 2026.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text:
Rental providers and their agents have a legal right to enter a rental property in certain circumstances.
Renters must generally allow entry when the rental provider or agent is legally entitled to enter and has provided the required notice.
Entry can include entering the property as a whole, including outdoor areas such as gardens.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text:
A rental provider or agent may enter a rental property for reasons including:
- General or routine inspection
- Repairs or other legal responsibilities
- Showing the property to prospective renters
- Showing the property to prospective buyers or lenders
- Having the property valued
- Taking photographs or videos for advertising
- Investigating whether the renter has breached legal or rental agreement obligations
- Certain inspections connected with VCAT family violence proceedings
The reason for entry determines the minimum notice period.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text:
The minimum written notice generally required is:
- General or routine inspection: 7 days
- Repairs or other legal responsibilities: 24 hours
- Showing the property to prospective renters, buyers or lenders: 48 hours
- Property valuation: 7 days
- Taking photographs or videos for advertising: 7 days
- Believing the renter has breached their obligations: 24 hours
- Certain VCAT family violence proceedings: 24 hours

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text:
A rental provider or agent can generally enter between 8 am and 6 pm on any day except a public holiday.
Entry outside these hours is only permitted if the renter agrees.
The agreement to enter outside the normal hours must be made no more than 7 days before the intended entry.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
section_title: WHEN A RENTER CAN REFUSE ENTRY
text:
A renter can refuse entry in circumstances such as:
- Entry is outside the permitted hours without the renter's agreement
- The day is a public holiday
- Required written notice was not provided
- Notice was not provided within the required timeframe
- A routine inspection has already occurred within the previous 6 months
- A prospective-renter inspection is being requested outside the permitted period
A renter may also seek an order from VCAT to limit entry times where there are good reasons for doing so.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text:
A general inspection is used to check the condition of the rental property and whether the renter is meeting their obligations.
A general inspection:
- Cannot normally occur during the first 3 months of the rental agreement
- Can occur no more than once every 6 months
- Requires at least 7 days' notice
The rental provider or agent can inspect all areas of the property during a general inspection.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
section_title: SHOWING THE PROPERTY TO PROSPECTIVE RENTERS
text:
A rental provider or agent can show the property to prospective renters when the current renter has given notice that they intend to leave or when the rental provider has given a notice to vacate.
An open inspection for prospective renters must occur no more than 21 days before the end of the rental agreement.
Prospective renters generally cannot be shown the property more than twice per week or for longer than one hour at a time unless the current renter agrees to different arrangements.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
section_title: SHOWING THE PROPERTY TO BUYERS OR LENDERS
text:
A rental provider or agent can show the property to prospective buyers when the property is going to be sold.
The renter must generally have been told that the owner intends to sell the property at least 14 days before the inspection.
The rental provider must make reasonable efforts to agree with the renter about suitable inspection days and times.
Prospective buyer inspections generally cannot occur more than twice per week or for longer than one hour each time unless the renter agrees otherwise.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text:
When a rental provider enters the property to hold a sales inspection for prospective buyers, the renter must generally receive compensation.
The compensation is the greater of:
- Half a day's rent
- $30

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text:
A rental provider or agent may enter to take photographs or videos for advertising after giving the required notice.
Renters can object in writing when photographs or videos would reveal certain personal, sensitive, valuable or identifying possessions.
If a renter makes a valid objection, the rental provider or agent must not include those items in the advertising material.
In some circumstances, the renter can request to see advertising photographs or videos before they are used.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
section_title: ENTRY WHEN THE RENTER IS NOT HOME
text:
A rental provider or agent can enter when the renter is not home if valid written notice has been provided or the renter has agreed to the entry.
The renter does not generally need to be present during a lawful entry.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
section_title: RENTERS DO NOT GENERALLY HAVE TO LEAVE
text: A rental provider may ask a renter to leave during an inspection or property showing, but a renter is generally not required to leave simply because the rental provider or agent is entering lawfully.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text:
A rental provider or agent must exercise entry rights reasonably.
They should not stay longer than necessary for the purpose of the visit unless the renter agrees.
Unreasonable entry or repeated unnecessary visits can be challenged.
A renter may apply to VCAT where entry rights are being misused or legal duties have been breached.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text: If a renter's belongings are damaged or taken while the rental provider or agent is on the property, the renter may be able to apply to VCAT for compensation.

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text:
Consumer Affairs Victoria provides forms including:
- Notice to renter of entry to rented premises
- Notice of intention to sell the property
- Notice of breach of duty to renter of rented premises

title: Rental Provider Entry Rights and Property Inspections
text: Rental provider entry rights and responsibilities are covered by sections 85–91A of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
The 15 categories are:
- Bathroom
- Electrical safety
- Heating
- Kitchen
- Laundry
- Lighting
- Locks
- Mould and damp
- Structural soundness
- Toilets
- Ventilation
- Vermin-proof bins
- Windows
- Window coverings
- Window covering anchors

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
The bathroom must have:
- A washbasin
- A shower or bath
- A reasonable supply of hot and cold water
Showers must generally have a shower head with a 3-star water efficiency rating.
If a 3-star shower head cannot be installed because of the property's age or another relevant reason, a 1- or 2-star shower head may be acceptable.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
Rental properties must have modern switchboards with circuit breakers and electrical safety switches.
Rental providers are responsible for engaging an electrician to ensure the property complies with the electrical safety standard.
The electrical safety minimum standard commenced on 29 March 2023.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
A rental property must have a fixed heater in good working order in the main living area.
For rental agreements entered into from 29 March 2023, the fixed heater must meet the applicable energy-efficiency requirement.
An energy-efficient fixed heater can include:
- A non-ducted air conditioner or heat pump with a 2-star or higher energy rating
- A gas space heater with a 2-star or higher energy rating
- Ducted heating or hydronic heating with an outlet in the main living area
- A domestic solid-fuel appliance such as a fireplace or wood-burning stove

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
A rental property must have a kitchen with:
- A dedicated cooking and food preparation area
- A sink in good working order
- A reasonable supply of hot and cold water
- A stovetop in good working order with at least two burners
If an oven is provided, it must be in good working order.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text: If the property has a laundry, it must be connected to a reasonable supply of hot and cold water.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
Interior rooms, corridors and hallways must have access to working lights.
The property must have access to natural light during the day.
At night, renters must have access to artificial light.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
External entry doors, other than screen doors, must have functional deadlocks or locks that:
- Can be unlocked with a key from outside
- Can be opened from inside without a key
The locks must provide reasonable security against external entry.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
All rooms must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure.
Structural causes of mould or damp may therefore require action by the rental provider.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text: The rental property must be structurally sound and weatherproof.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
The toilet must:
- Be in good working order
- Be connected to an appropriate sewerage or wastewater system
- Be located in a separate room or an appropriate combined room such as a bathroom-laundry

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
Rental properties must have adequate ventilation in all relevant rooms.
This includes:
- Habitable rooms
- Bathroom
- Shower
- Toilet
- Laundry
The applicable ventilation requirements can depend on the type of property and the Building Code of Australia.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
Rental providers must supply rubbish and recycling bins for renters.
The bins must:
- Be vermin-proof
- Meet relevant council collection standards

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
All external windows that can be opened must have functioning latches.
The latches must secure the windows against external entry.
Openable windows must also be able to remain in an open or closed position.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
Rooms likely to be used as bedrooms or living areas must have curtains or blinds.
Window coverings must:
- Be capable of being closed
- Block light
- Provide privacy

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
From 1 December 2025, all corded internal window coverings, such as blinds and curtains, must have an anchor installed to secure the cords and prevent them from forming loops.
This requirement is a current minimum standard.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
Rental properties must meet the minimum standards before they are advertised or offered for rent.
For existing rental agreements, the minimum standards in Schedule 4 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 generally apply when the agreement:
- Started on or after 29 March 2021, or
- Started before 29 March 2021 and became a periodic agreement on or after 29 March 2021
Different rules can apply to rooming houses and other specialised accommodation.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
section_title: IF A PROPERTY DOES NOT MEET THE STANDARDS
text:
Renters should inspect a property before signing a rental agreement.
If the property does not meet the minimum standards, the renter can ask the rental provider to make repairs or changes before signing or moving in.
If the renter has already signed the agreement but has not moved in, the renter can generally:
- End the rental agreement, or
- Move in and request an urgent repair
If the renter is already living in the property, failure to meet a minimum standard may also amount to an urgent repair issue.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
New minimum rental standards relating to energy efficiency are scheduled to be introduced from 1 March 2027.
These future requirements should not be treated as current requirements in the knowledge base as of 4 September 2026.

title: Rental Properties - Minimum Standards
text:
The minimum standards are supported by the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021.
Relevant provisions include:
- Section 65A – Occupation of rented premises that do not comply with minimum standards
- Section 65B – Advertisement of premises that do not comply with minimum standards
- Section 72 – Urgent repairs
- Section 77 – Payment of rent into Rent Special Account
- Schedule 4 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 – Rental minimum standards

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
Before moving into a rental property, renters should check that the property meets the Victorian rental minimum standards.
Rental providers and agents are responsible for ensuring the property meets the applicable minimum standards when it is advertised or offered for rent and before the renter moves in.
If the property does not meet the minimum standards, the renter can ask the rental provider to make the required repairs or changes before signing the rental agreement or before moving in.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
Before a renter moves in, the rental provider or agent must provide relevant information and documents.
This can include:
- A copy of the rental agreement if it is in writing
- The Renters Guide
- A phone number for urgent repairs outside normal business hours
- The rental provider or agent's full name
- A postal address for sending documents
- An email address where electronic communication has been agreed
- A set of keys for each renter who signed the agreement
- A condition report

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
A condition report is a record of the property's condition at the beginning of a rental agreement.
It should record the condition of:
- Rooms
- Fittings
- Fixtures
- Items inside the property
- Items outside the property
Anything that is unclean, damaged or not working should be recorded.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
section_title: CONDITION REPORT PROVIDED BY THE RENTAL PROVIDER
text:
The rental provider or agent must prepare and sign the condition report.
They must provide the renter with:
- Two copies of the signed report before moving in, or
- One electronic copy when provided electronically
The renter should carefully inspect the property before completing their part of the report.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
The renter should check the condition report carefully and add comments where the report is incomplete or inaccurate.
The renter should record:
- Existing damage
- Marks or stains
- Broken or damaged fittings
- Items that are not working
- Areas that are not reasonably clean
- Other relevant defects or problems
The renter should then sign the completed report and return one copy to the rental provider or agent.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
The renter must return the completed and signed condition report within 5 business days of moving into the property.
Weekends and public holidays are not counted as business days.
If the renter was not given a condition report before moving in, they can complete their own condition report and provide it to the rental provider or agent within 5 business days of moving in.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
Renters should take photographs of the property's condition when they move in.
Photographs are particularly useful for documenting pre-existing damage.
Photos should be:
- Dated
- Clearly labelled
- Kept with the condition report
Digital photographs can be used.
Keeping photographic evidence can help resolve later disputes about damage, cleaning or bond claims.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
The condition report can be important evidence if there is a dispute about:
- Bond claims
- Cleaning
- Property damage
- Missing items
- Responsibility for repairs
Renters should keep their copy of the completed condition report for the entire rental agreement.
The rental provider or agent should also retain their copy.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
section_title: REPAIRS IDENTIFIED IN THE CONDITION REPORT
text:
If a condition report identifies something that needs repair, the report can provide written notice of the issue to the rental provider.
If the required repair is not completed within a reasonable period, the renter may be able to apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repair.
Urgent repairs are subject to separate rules and should be reported as soon as possible.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
section_title: IF THE PROPERTY DOES NOT MEET MINIMUM STANDARDS
text:
If the property does not meet the minimum rental standards before the renter moves in, the renter can request that the rental provider make the necessary repairs or changes.
If the rental agreement has already been signed but the renter has not moved in, the renter can generally:
- End the rental agreement immediately without fees by notifying the rental provider that the property does not meet minimum standards, or
- Move in and request urgent repairs
If a property falls below the minimum standards during the rental agreement, the renter can contact the rental provider or agent and request an urgent repair.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
A rental provider or agent may require a renter to pay a bond, subject to Victorian rental law.
The maximum bond is generally one month's rent unless the weekly rent is more than $900.
In some circumstances, the rental provider may apply to VCAT for an increase to the bond limit.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
If the renter pays the bond to the rental provider or agent, it must generally be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days of the rental provider or agent receiving it.
The RTBA holds the bond in trust until it is claimed.
The RTBA sends the renter a receipt containing the bond number.
Renters should keep their bond number in a safe place.
If a renter does not receive a bond receipt within 15 business days of making payment, they should contact the RTBA.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
Renters and rental providers can agree to exchange certain documents and information electronically.
This can include:
- Rental agreements
- Condition reports
- Information about rental rights
- Inspection notices
- Other notices and documents
Where electronic communication is used, the parties should keep copies of important documents.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
Renters should retain important records from the beginning of the tenancy, including:
- Rental agreement
- Condition report
- Photographs
- Bond receipt and bond number
- Rent records
- Repair requests
- Communications with the rental provider or agent
- Notices received
These records can be useful if a dispute occurs later.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
section_title: CONDITION REPORT AT THE END OF THE AGREEMENT
text:
When the rental agreement ends, the rental provider or agent must complete the exit condition report section of the original condition report within 10 days.
The renter must be present or have been given a reasonable opportunity to attend.
The exit condition report records the condition of the property at the end of the tenancy.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
The original condition report and photographs can be used as evidence when determining responsibility for damage or cleaning.
A rental provider may use the condition report to support a bond claim for new damage, repairs, additional cleaning or missing items.
Normal fair wear and tear should be distinguished from new damage.

title: Moving Into a Rental Property and Condition Reports
text:
Condition reports are covered by relevant provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997.
Consumer Affairs Victoria identifies sections including:
- Section 35
- Section 97
- Section 148
- Section 206O

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
A renter who wants to end their rental agreement can:
- Reach an agreement with the rental provider about leaving, or
- Give a formal written notice of intention to vacate.
A notice of intention to vacate is a formal statement that the renter wants to end the rental agreement.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
section_title: LEAVING AT THE END OF A RENTAL AGREEMENT
text:
A renter generally needs to give 28 days' notice if they want to leave at the end of their rental agreement.
For a fixed-term agreement, the renter should ensure the notice does not specify a date earlier than the agreement's end date unless a lawful reason for early termination applies.
Since 25 November 2025, a fixed-term agreement generally becomes a periodic agreement when it ends if neither party enters a new fixed-term agreement and the rental provider does not give a valid notice to vacate.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
The renter must give the notice of intention to vacate in writing.
The official Consumer Affairs Victoria form is recommended:
Notice of intention to vacate rented premises by renter.
The notice should clearly state:
- The renter's intention to leave
- The address of the rented premises
- The date the renter intends to leave
- Relevant details required by the form

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
A renter can deliver the notice by:
- Post
- Electronic communication, such as email, where permitted
- Hand delivery to the rental provider
If the notice is posted, the renter should allow enough time for delivery.
Renters should keep evidence that the notice was sent or delivered.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
section_title: LEAVING EARLY WITHOUT BREAKING THE AGREEMENT
text:
There are specific circumstances where a renter can end a rental agreement before the usual end date without breaking the agreement.
The applicable notice period depends on the reason.
Examples include:
- The property becomes unfit for human habitation or is destroyed to an extent that makes it unsafe
- The rental provider breaches certain VCAT orders
- The rental provider repeatedly breaches certain duties
- The rental provider refuses requested disability-related changes
- The renter needs temporary crisis accommodation
- The renter needs special or personal care
- The renter is moving into social housing
- Certain notices to vacate have been given by the rental provider
Some reasons require documentary evidence.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
section_title: NOTICE PERIODS FOR CERTAIN EARLY-ENDING REASONS
text:
Depending on the circumstances, the required notice can be:
- Immediate
- 14 days
- 28 days
The renter should check the specific reason and evidence requirements before relying on a shorter notice period.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
Leaving a property before the rental agreement ends without a lawful reason or without the required agreement can amount to breaking the rental agreement.
A renter who breaks the agreement may have to pay reasonable costs caused by the early termination.
Potential costs can include:
- Rent until a new renter moves in or the agreement ends, subject to the law
- Advertising costs
- Reasonable costs of finding a new renter
- Other permitted costs resulting from the early termination
A rental provider cannot simply charge any amount they choose.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
section_title: COSTS A RENTER DOES NOT HAVE TO PAY
text:
A renter generally does not have to pay costs that are unreasonable or unrelated to the early termination.
The rental provider should take reasonable steps to reduce their losses.
A renter can dispute claimed costs if they believe the amount is incorrect or unreasonable.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
A renter experiencing severe hardship may apply to VCAT to end a fixed-term rental agreement without having to pay the usual costs associated with breaking the agreement.
Examples of circumstances that may contribute to severe hardship include:
- Significant loss of income
- Serious personal circumstances
- Serious medical circumstances
- Family tragedy
VCAT considers the circumstances of the renter and the rental provider when deciding an application.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
Before leaving, renters should:
- Clean the property reasonably
- Remove their belongings
- Remove rubbish
- Return all required keys
- Pay rent and other amounts that are lawfully owed
- Complete any required final inspection process
- Keep copies of important rental records
- Take photographs of the property's final condition
Renters should compare the property's final condition with the original condition report.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
Renters are generally responsible for damage they caused but not for normal fair wear and tear.
Fair wear and tear can result from ordinary use and the natural ageing of a property.
The original condition report and photographs can help determine whether damage existed before the renter moved in or occurred during the tenancy.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
A final inspection can be used to assess the condition of the property when the renter leaves.
The original condition report should be used as evidence when comparing the property's condition at the beginning and end of the rental agreement.
The renter should have a reasonable opportunity to attend the final inspection where required.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
After the rental agreement ends, the rental bond can be claimed through the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA).
The rental provider must generally start a bond claim within 14 days after the rental agreement ends unless the renter starts the claim first.
The renter can initiate the bond claim and can dispute a rental provider's claim.
Fair wear and tear cannot be claimed as damage from the bond.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
Renters should return all keys, remotes, access devices and other items that belong to the rental provider.
Failure to return keys or access devices may result in costs where permitted by law.
Renters should keep evidence that keys and access devices were returned.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
Renters remain responsible for rent and other lawful amounts up to the end of the rental agreement or until another lawful arrangement applies.
Rent should not simply be stopped because a renter has given notice.
If there is a dispute about money owed, the renter should seek advice rather than withholding rent without a lawful basis.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
If a renter gives a notice of intention to vacate and later decides to stay, they should tell the rental provider as soon as possible and provide a written request to withdraw the notice.
The rental provider or agent does not have to agree to withdraw the notice.
If the rental provider does not agree, the renter may apply to VCAT in appropriate circumstances.
Unless VCAT allows the renter to stay longer, the renter must generally leave by the date stated in the original notice.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
section_title: IF THE RENTER DOES NOT LEAVE
text:
If a renter gives notice but does not leave by the required date, the rental provider can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the renter to move out.
A rental provider cannot personally evict a renter.
Legal eviction requires the appropriate VCAT process and enforcement steps.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
Renters should remove all personal belongings before leaving.
If goods are left behind, specific Victorian rules apply to how the rental provider must deal with those goods.
Renters should therefore arrange removal of their belongings before returning possession of the property.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
This document reflects Victorian rental information checked on 5 September 2026.
Rental laws can change over time.
The Consumer Affairs Victoria rental-law changes page identifies further changes scheduled for 13 October 2026.
Those future changes should not be treated as current requirements in this document.

title: Ending the Rental Agreement and Moving Out
text:
Relevant provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 include:
- Section 91Z – Notice of intention to vacate
- Section 91ZA – Notice to have no effect in certain circumstances
- Section 91ZB – Reduced period of notice in certain circumstances
- Section 91ZZN – Form of notice of intention to vacate
Breaking a rental agreement is also governed by relevant provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act 1997.
